{{short description|Mathematical theory}}
'''Wiman–Valiron theory''' is a mathematical theory invented by [[Anders Wiman]] as a tool to study the behavior of
arbitrary [[entire function]]s. After the work of Wiman, the theory was developed by other mathematicians,
and extended to
more general classes of analytic functions. The main result of the theory is an [[Asymptotic analysis|asymptotic formula]] for the function
and its derivatives near the point where the maximum modulus of this function is attained.

== Maximal term and central index ==

By definition, an entire function can be represented by a [[power series]] which is convergent for all complex {{tmath| z }}:
: <math>f(z)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_nz^n.</math>

The terms of this series tend to 0 as {{tmath| n\to\infty }}, so for each <math>z</math> there is a term of maximal modulus. This term depends on {{tmath|1= r := \vert z \vert }}.
Its modulus is called the ''maximal term'' of the series:
: <math>\mu(r,f)=\max_k |a_k|r^k=:|a_n|r^n,\quad r\geq 0.</math>

Here <math>n</math> is the exponent for which the maximum is attained; if there are several maximal terms, we define <math>n</math> as the largest exponent of them. This number <math>n</math> depends on <math>r</math>, it is denoted by <math>n(r,f)</math> and is called the ''central index''.

Let
: <math> M(r,f)=\max\{ |f(z)|: |z|\leq r \}</math>
be the maximum modulus of the function {{tmath| f }}.
[[Cauchy's integral formula#Consequences|Cauchy's inequality]] implies that <math>\mu(r,f)\leq M(r,f)</math> for all <math>r\geq 0</math>.
The converse estimate <math>M(r,f)\leq (\mu(r,f))^{1+\epsilon}</math> was first proved by [[Emile Borel|Borel]], and a more precise estimate due to [[Anders Wiman|Wiman]] reads<ref name="wim1">{{cite journal |first=A. |last=Wiman |authorlink=Anders Wiman |title=Über den Zusammenhang zwischen dem Maximalbetrage einer analytischen Funktion und dem grössten Gliede der zugehörigen taylor'schen Reihe |journal=Acta Mathematica |year=1914 |volume=37 |pages=305–326 (German) |doi= 10.1007/BF02401837 |doi-access=free |s2cid= 121155803 }}</ref>
: <math>M(r,f)\leq \mu(r,f)\left(\log\mu(r,f)\right)^{1/2+\epsilon},</math>
in the sense that for every <math>\epsilon>0</math> there exist arbitrarily large values of <math>r</math> for which this inequality holds. In fact, it was shown by Valiron that the above relation holds for "most" values of <math>r</math>: the exceptional set <math>E</math> for which it does not hold has finite logarithmic measure:
: <math>\int_E\frac{dr}{r}<\infty.</math>

Improvements of these inequality were subject of much research in the 20th century.<ref name="hay">{{cite journal |first=W. |last=Hayman |authorlink=Walter Hayman |title=The local growth of power series: a survey of the Wiman–Valiron method |journal=[[Canadian Mathematical Bulletin]] |volume= 17 |year= 1974 |issue=3 |pages=317–358 |doi=10.4153/CMB-1974-064-0 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

== Main asymptotic formula ==

The following result of Wiman<ref name="wim2">{{cite journal |first=A. |last=Wiman |authorlink=Anders Wiman |title=Über den Zusammenhang zwischen dem Maximalbetrage einer analytischen Funktion und dem grössten Betrage bei gegebenem Argumente der Funktion |journal=Acta Mathematica |year=1916 |volume=41 |pages=1–28 (German) |doi=10.1007/BF02422938 |doi-access=free |s2cid=122491610 }}</ref> is fundamental for various applications: let <math>z_r</math> be the point for which the maximum in the definition of <math>M(r,f)</math> is attained; by the [[Maximum Principle]] we have {{tmath|1= \vert z_r \vert = r }}. It turns out that <math>f(z)</math> behaves near the point <math>z_r</math> like a monomial: there are arbitrarily large values of <math>r</math> such that the formula
: <math>f(z)=(1+o(1))\left(\frac{z}{z_r}\right)^{n(r,f)}f(z_r),</math>
holds in the disk
: <math>|z-z_r|<\frac{r}{\left(n(r)\right)^{1/2+\epsilon}}.</math>

Here <math>\epsilon>0</math> is an arbitrary positive number, and the o(1) refers to {{tmath| r\to\infty,\; r\not\in E }}, where <math>E</math> is the exceptional set described above. This disk is usually called the ''Wiman–Valiron disk''.

== Applications ==

The formula for <math>f(z)</math> for <math>z</math> near <math>z_r</math> can be differentiated so we have an asymptotic relation
: <math>f^{(m)}(z)=(1+o(1))\left(\frac{n(r)}{z}\right)^m\left(\frac{r}{z_r}\right)^{n(r)}f(z_r).</math>

This is useful for studies of entire solutions of differential equations.

Another important application is due to [[Georges Valiron|Valiron]]
<ref name="val">{{cite book |first=G. |last=Valiron |authorlink=Georges Valiron |title=Lectures on the general theory of integral functions |year=1949 |publisher=Chelsea, reprint of the 1923 ed. |place=NY }}</ref> who noticed that the image of the Wiman–Valiron disk contains a "large" annulus ({{tmath| \{ z:r_1 < \vert z \vert < r_2\} }} where both <math>r_1</math> and <math>r_2/r_1</math> are arbitrarily large). This implies the important theorem of Valiron that there are arbitrarily large discs in the plane in which the inverse branches of an entire function can be defined. A quantitative version of this statement is known as the [[Bloch's theorem (complex variables)|Bloch theorem]].

This theorem of Valiron has further applications in holomorphic dynamics: it is used in the proof of the fact that the [[escaping set]] of an entire function is not empty.

== Later development ==

In 1938, Macintyre<ref name="mac">{{cite journal |first=A. |last=Macintyre |title=Wiman's method and the "flat regions" of integral functions |journal=Quarterly Journal of Mathematics |year=1938 |pages=81–88 |doi=10.1093/qmath/os-9.1.81 }}</ref> found that one can get rid of the central index and of power series itself in this theory. Macintyre replaced the central index by the quantity
: <math>a(r,f):=r\frac{M'(r,f)}{M(r,f)}</math>
and proved the main relation in the form
: <math>f^{(m)}(z)=(1+o(1))\left(\frac{a(r,f)}{z}\right)^m\left(\frac{z}{z_r}\right)^{a(r,f)}f(z_r)\quad\mbox{for}
\quad|z-z_r|\leq\frac{r}{(a(r,f))^{1/2+\epsilon}}.</math>

This statement does not mention the power series, but the assumption that <math>f</math> is entire was used by Macintyre.

The final generalization was achieved by Bergweiler, Rippon and Stallard<ref name="brs">{{cite journal |first1=W. |last1=Bergweiler |first2=Ph.| last2=Rippon |first3=G. |last3=Stallard |title=Dynamics of meromorphic functions with direct or logarithmic singularities |journal=Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society |year=2008 |volume=97 |issue=2 |pages=368–400 |doi=10.1112/plms/pdn007|arxiv=0704.2712 |s2cid=16873707 }}</ref> who showed that this relation persists for every unbounded analytic function <math>f</math> defined in an arbitrary unbounded region <math>D</math> in the complex plane, under the only assumption that <math>|f(z)|</math> is bounded for {{tmath| z\in\partial D }}. The key statement which makes this generalization possible is that the Wiman–Valiron disk is actually contained in <math>D</math>
for all non-exceptional {{tmath| r }}.
